title: Biblical Commentary on the Books of Samuel
author: Carl Friedrich Keil; Franz Delitzsch (trans. James Martin)
allowedUseNotes: Public-domain 19th-century commentary (original German editions 1864-1875; this English translation published 1866, pre-1928). May be cited, quoted in short excerpt, or paraphrased freely with attribution; no full-chapter reproduction needed per this project's own tighter internal policy regardless.
summary:
Classic 19th-century verse-by-verse critical-conservative commentary on 1-2 Samuel, part of the larger multi-volume Keil-Delitzsch Commentary on the Old Testament (the Samuel volume's exegetical work is Keil's; Delitzsch is credited on the original title page as the series' co-author/editor). On 1 Samuel 31:12-13, Keil explains the men of Jabesh-gilead's burning of Saul's and his sons' bodies as arising from the specific circumstances rather than ordinary Israelite funerary custom: the bodies had already been mutilated (decapitated) and displayed on Beth-shan's wall, making a normal burial impossible in the usual sense, and the men of Jabesh feared further desecration if the Philistines followed up their victory and reached Jabesh. Keil also reports and rejects an older Targumic/rabbinic reading (also discussed in the Gill source card) that the 'burning' refers to ceremonial burning of spices over the bodies rather than cremation of the flesh itself, arguing the Hebrew phrasing here differs from the idiom used for that funerary-spice custom elsewhere (e.g., the 'very great burning' made for King Asa, 2 Chronicles 16:14). On 2 Samuel 1:1-10, Keil addresses the Amalekite messenger's claim to have killed Saul at the king's own request, directly against 1 Samuel 31:3-5's own narration of Saul falling on his own sword unaided. Keil's reading: the only part of the messenger's account that can be taken as certainly true is that he came upon Saul already lying dead on the field and stripped the crown from his head and the armlet from his arm; the claim to have delivered the death-blow himself is judged an invented embellishment, told to secure a reward and a welcome from the new king. Keil also notes the narrative gives no way to determine whether the Amalekite's arrival at Ziklag preceded or followed David's own return from pursuing the Amalekite raiders (1 Samuel 30), only that the two are narrated as close in time.

Researcher pass (2026-08-08, M5 citation-gap closure) extended coverage to 2 Samuel 3-4. On 2 Samuel 3:27-30 (Joab's killing of Abner), Keil reads the text's own stated reason — blood vengeance for Asahel (3:27, 30) — as the account's actual, plainly reported motive, consistent with his general practice of not positing a later apologetic redactional shaping of the narrative; this project cites him for the blood-vengeance scholarlyView on claim-abner-killing, not for the separate rival-elimination-for-command reading (which this pass could not confirm as Keil's own point). On 2 Samuel 3:31-39 (David's mourning and the chapter's close), Keil frames the section as David 'declaring his abhorrence of Joab's crime' through solemn mourning and public curse — read as a straightforward, genuine response to a real event rather than a literary device shaped to defend David retrospectively, which this project treats as the checkable representative of claim-public-response's 'plain report' scholarlyView (Keil's own commentary predates, and does not engage with, the 20th-century apologetic-source-critical framework McCarter later proposes — its plain, event-level exegetical stance is cited here as substantively occupying that pole of the dispute, not as a direct rebuttal of McCarter). On 2 Samuel 4:6 (how Rechab and Baanah gained entry to kill Ish-bosheth), Keil discusses both textual traditions directly: he reads the Masoretic Text's own wording as the two men entering the house 'fetching wheat' (i.e., under the pretext of fetching wheat, probably for their soldiers) and striking Ish-bosheth in the abdomen, and separately reports the Septuagint's longer, different account — a female doorkeeper sifting wheat who grows drowsy and falls asleep, letting the two slip past her — as the reading he describes but does not adopt. This project cites Keil for the Masoretic-Text view directly (view-ishbosheth-entry-mt) and for reporting/describing the Septuagint's contents (view-ishbosheth-entry-lxx), since he is the only source in the project's bibliography currently found to lay out both readings side by side.
